rooms.name: Petersburg
rooms.description: The city is repeatedly referenced as the central arena where characters converge: Svidrigaïlov arrives after his wife’s funeral, Luzhin pursues marriage and status, and the police investigation unfolds. It is depicted through its lodging houses, streets, canals, and crowded quarters rather than through grand landmarks. Petersburg is also described as a town of officials and students, a place of clubs, parades, and bureaucracy. The city’s density enables both chance encounters and constant surveillance.

It is associated with his garret room under the roof of a tall, five-storied building. The place is tied to his avoidance of his landlady and his shame about debt. It feels like a cramped, precarious foothold in the city rather than a home.

rooms.description: A cramped attic room where Raskolnikov has been ill and delirious, with a table where money lies and a door he carefully latches and unlatches. It connects directly to the lodging house staircase and the landlady’s kitchen area, allowing him to slip out unnoticed. The space functions as a private refuge but also a pressure-cooker for his feverish resolve. It is the starting point of his wandering and the place others expect to find him confined to bed.

rooms.description: A rough quarter characterized by crowded streets and alleys filled with trading and working-class people. It is close to many establishments of bad character and numerous pot-houses, contributing to a pervasive stench and drunkenness. The area’s social mix makes even extreme shabbiness unremarkable. It forms the grim backdrop to Raskolnikov’s poverty and disgust.

The environment is filled with bustle, construction materials, and oppressive airlessness. He is shouted at from a passing wagon, prompting panic about his noticeable hat. The street amplifies his paranoia and physical weakness.

It is inhabited by a mix of working people and petty clerks, with constant traffic through two gates and two courtyards. Multiple door-keepers are employed, increasing the risk of being noticed. The building’s layout and movement make it feel like a maze of surveillance and opportunity.

He knows it well and finds comfort in its concealment, as darkness reduces the threat of inquisitive eyes. The staircase is interrupted by porters moving furniture on the fourth storey. It functions as a covert route through the building’s social machinery.

It is a place of listening, waiting, and heightened nerves.

A cotton curtain covers the doorway to the inner room where the bed and chest of drawers are kept. The flat is both domestic and transactional, arranged to control access and conceal valuables.

Raskolnikov has never looked into it directly, but he watches the curtain and listens to the sounds of unlocking. The room is implied to hold valuables or at least the mechanisms of storage and secrecy. Its partial concealment makes it feel like the flat’s private core.

It marks a shift from frantic walking to impulsive retreat indoors.

It becomes a temporary refuge where his thoughts briefly clear, though unease remains.

It is a transitional corridor for his aimless yet driven movement, with passers-by and the oppressive heat pressing in. His dizziness and feverish energy intensify as he walks. The street frames his determination to end everything “to-day.”

Tea is served, and in a farther room a group of men drink champagne, including (apparently) Zametov. The view includes a row of houses, a distant attic window catching the last light, and the canal below. The bridge becomes the site of a public emergency when a tall woman throws herself into the canal. It is also a turning point where Raskolnikov’s energy collapses into apathy and he decides to go to the police office.

It becomes the medium of a suicide attempt, swallowing the woman briefly before she resurfaces and drifts with the current. The canal’s steps allow quick access for rescue, and the embankment provides a place to lay the victim. For Raskolnikov, the water is associated with disgust and a rejected “way out.”

It serves as an impromptu emergency staging area, ringed by police and onlookers. The woman regains consciousness here, coughing and sneezing, wiping her wet dress. The embankment anchors the scene in stark physicality and public scrutiny.

Changes are noted: a window frame removed on the first landing and a newly painted, shut-up flat on the second storey. The staircase is a memory-laden route, retracing the path of the crime. It leads directly to the now-open, renovated murder flat.

The new white wallpaper with lilac flowers replaces the old dirty yellow, irritating Raskolnikov as if the scene is being erased. He sits on the window-sill, wanders into the inner room where the strong box and furniture had been, and fixates on the bell’s cracked note. His repeated ringing and questions about blood provoke suspicion and lead to calls to take him to the police station.

The same new wallpaper covers it, and a visible patch in the corner marks where the case of ikons used to stand. Raskolnikov inspects the corner and the window, as if measuring the absence of objects and the rewriting of the scene. The room reinforces his fixation on the physical traces of the crime.

Here, Raskolnikov is questioned about his presence and behavior, identifies himself and his address, and is accused of being a rogue. The workmen come down and recount his strange remarks about the washed-away blood and his insistence on the police station. The scene ends with a porter physically ejecting him into the street.

It is invoked as the destination where he could explain himself, and others suggest taking him there after his behavior in the murder flat. Though he does not reach it within this excerpt, it exerts a gravitational pull on his decisions. The police office represents formal authority and the looming possibility of confession or arrest.

rooms.atmosphere: Foreboding and inevitable; an institutional endpoint hovering just out of reach.

rooms.name: Shil’s house, flat Number 14 (Raskolnikov’s stated address)
rooms.description: A residence Raskolnikov cites to identify himself to the porters, described as not far from the pawnbroker’s building. It functions as a verifiable point of reference—“ask the porter, he knows me”—rather than an active setting in the scene. The address anchors his identity in the neighborhood and suggests proximity between his lodging and the crime location. It is mentioned in a detached, dreamy tone that contrasts with the suspicion around him.
exits: Implied building entrance and porter access
events: Raskolnikov gives his name and address while being questioned at the gateway.
rooms.atmosphere: Matter-of-fact and bureaucratic; a thin shield of normalcy amid accusation.

rooms.name: Cross-roads / thoroughfare near the tenement (where Raskolnikov hesitates)
rooms.description: A junction where Raskolnikov stands in the middle of the thoroughfare, uncertain whether to go to the police station. The stones and silence feel dead to him, as if the city offers no guidance. From here he sees, two hundred yards away, a crowd gathered around a carriage with a light in the street. The cross-roads becomes a moment of suspended decision before he moves toward the commotion.
exits: Toward the police office
Back toward the tenement gateway
Toward the distant crowd and carriage
events: Raskolnikov hesitates, then heads toward a crowd gathered around a carriage.
rooms.atmosphere: Eerily silent and fatalistic; a pause before the next shock.

rooms.name: Road (accident scene in the middle of the road)
rooms.description: A public roadway where an elegant carriage with spirited grey horses has stopped after running over a man. A crowd gathers tightly around the wheels while police hold the front line and illuminate the injured man with a lantern. The scene is chaotic, with shouting, exclamations, and the coachman repeatedly lamenting the misfortune. It functions as the immediate crisis point that draws Raskolnikov into action and sets the subsequent movement to Kozel’s house in motion.
exits: To Kozel’s house (about thirty yards away)
To the police station (discussed as an option for taking the injured man)
To the hospital (discussed as an option for taking the injured man)
events: Marmeladov is found run over and bleeding
Raskolnikov identifies Marmeladov and urges immediate help
Decision made to carry Marmeladov to his lodging in Kozel’s house
rooms.atmosphere: Noisy, urgent, and public; a spectacle of misfortune with anxious authority and morbid curiosity.

rooms.name: Kozel’s house
rooms.description: A nearby building owned by Kozel, described as a rich German, located only a short distance from the accident. It serves as the destination where Marmeladov is carried for immediate care rather than being taken to the hospital. The house contains a staircase and multiple lodgings, including the cramped room of Marmeladov’s family. It becomes the setting for the deathbed scene and the gathering of neighbors and lodgers.
exits: Back to the road (accident scene)
Upstairs to Marmeladov family’s room
Downstairs to the yard and street
events: Marmeladov is carried into the building and taken upstairs
rooms.atmosphere: Crowded tenement life; close quarters and communal intrusion under stress.

rooms.name: Marmeladov family’s little room (in Kozel’s house)
rooms.description: A cramped, impoverished room where Katerina Ivanovna paces from window to stove, coughing and talking to herself and her children. The door to the stairs is often left open to relieve tobacco smoke drifting in from other rooms, though it worsens her coughing fits. The room contains a sofa used as a bed, a stove corner where the children kneel to pray, and makeshift household items for constant washing and mending. It becomes a death chamber when Marmeladov is brought in, drawing in police, a doctor, a priest, and a crowd of lodgers.
exits: To the staircase/passage outside the room
To the inner rooms of the flat (where other lodgers are)
To the window (overlooking yard/light source)
events: Marmeladov is carried in and placed on the sofa
Doctor is summoned and declares Marmeladov will die imminently
Priest arrives and administers confession/sacrament
Marmeladov dies after recognizing Sonia; Sonia embraces him
Raskolnikov gives Katerina Ivanovna twenty roubles for assistance
rooms.atmosphere: Stifling, smoky, and claustrophobic; a mix of poverty, grief, spectacle, and frantic caretaking under the shadow of death.

rooms.name: Staircase and passage outside Marmeladov’s room (Kozel’s house)
rooms.description: A shared corridor and stairwell where smoke from other rooms drifts and where crowds gather to watch the accident’s aftermath. The doorway becomes a bottleneck as lodgers press in, then retreat under Katerina Ivanovna’s fury and the policeman’s attempts to clear space. It is also the route for arrivals: the doctor, the priest, Polenka returning with news, and Sonia entering timidly. Later, Raskolnikov exits through this space and is stopped by Polenka at the bottom of the stairs.
exits: Into Marmeladov family’s room
Into inner rooms of the flat (lodgers’ rooms)
Downstairs to the yard and street
items: Open door to stairs (used for ventilation)
characters: Nikodim Fomitch (arrives later to give instructions)
events: Spectators surge and are pushed back
Doctor and priest arrive through the crowd
Polenka meets Raskolnikov on the stairs and asks his name/address
rooms.atmosphere: Pressing, voyeuristic, and noisy; communal curiosity colliding with private tragedy.

rooms.name: Yard (dimly lit, outside Kozel’s house)
rooms.description: A courtyard area providing a dim light that reaches the bottom of the staircase. It is where Polenka stops Raskolnikov after he leaves the deathbed scene, and where their intimate exchange occurs. The yard’s faint illumination contrasts with the emotional intensity of the child’s gratitude and grief. It also functions as a transitional space between the tenement interior and the street.
exits: To the staircase up into the house
To the street outside
items: Dim ambient light source (from the yard)
events: Polenka asks Raskolnikov’s name and address
Polenka kisses and hugs Raskolnikov; he asks her to pray for him
rooms.atmosphere: Quiet, dim, and tender; a brief refuge of human warmth after chaos.

rooms.name: Street (outside Kozel’s house / general city street at night)
rooms.description: The street is where Raskolnikov emerges after Marmeladov’s death, spattered with blood, and where he speaks with Nikodim Fomitch. It is also the route he takes to the bridge and later to Potchinkov’s house and back toward his own lodging. The street is portrayed as oppressive and airless, with the sense that even open streets feel like shut-up rooms. It serves as the connective tissue between major locations and emotional states.
exits: To the bridge
To Potchinkov’s house
To Raskolnikov’s lodging/garret
To Kozel’s house
events: Nikodim Fomitch notes Raskolnikov’s blood-stained waistcoat
Raskolnikov walks in a surge of renewed resolve
Razumihin escorts Raskolnikov home and later escorts the women to their lodgings
rooms.atmosphere: Restless and oppressive; a city that feels close and suffocating even outdoors.

rooms.name: Bridge (spot where a woman had jumped in)
rooms.description: A bridge where Raskolnikov stops late at night and stands at the exact spot of an earlier suicide attempt. He delivers a triumphant internal monologue about rejecting phantoms and embracing life, reason, and strength. The bridge becomes a symbolic threshold between despair and renewed will. From here he decides to go to Razumihin at Potchinkov’s house.
exits: Back to the street
Toward Potchinkov’s house
items: Bridge railing/edge (implied by the referenced jumping spot)
events: Raskolnikov declares he is done with imaginary terrors and will test his strength
rooms.atmosphere: Nighttime, reflective, and defiant; a moment of self-reinvention over dark water.

rooms.name: Potchinkov’s house
rooms.description: A building near the bridge where Razumihin is lodging, known to the porter who directs visitors upstairs. It contains a lively gathering in Razumihin’s fairly large room, with loud conversation audible from the stairs. The entry area includes a screen behind which servants prepare samovars and food brought from the landlady’s kitchen. It serves as a social hub and a point where Raskolnikov briefly appears to acknowledge Razumihin’s “bet” and take medicine.
exits: To the street
Upstairs to Razumihin’s room
To the entry area with servants and samovars
items: Bottles, plates, dishes of pie and savouries
events: Raskolnikov refuses to join the party and is given a medicinal powder
Razumihin decides to escort Raskolnikov home
rooms.atmosphere: Boisterous and crowded; convivial noise contrasted with Raskolnikov’s fragility.

rooms.name: Razumihin’s room (at Potchinkov’s house)
rooms.description: A fairly large room hosting a gathering of about fifteen people engaged in animated, often nonsensical discussion. The door stands wide open to the stairs, letting the noise spill into the building. Razumihin is visibly drunk and on edge, close to coming to blows with his guests. The room functions as a social counterpoint to the surrounding misery and illness elsewhere.
exits: To the stairs/landing outside (door wide open)
To the entry area with servants and samovars
items: Alcohol (implied by Razumihin’s condition and the party)
General party provisions (tea/food implied via entry supplies)

Zossimov is fetched from the party
rooms.atmosphere: Loud, argumentative, and intoxicated; social heat and volatility.

rooms.name: Raskolnikov’s garret (his lodging under the roof)
rooms.description: A small, tomb-like room under the roof that serves as Raskolnikov’s living space and bedchamber, with a sofa used for sleeping. A light is seen through the crack in the door late at night, revealing unexpected visitors: his mother and sister waiting anxiously. The room becomes crowded with Razumihin, Nastasya, and later Zossimov, and is the site of repeated fainting and tense family conversation. Its oppressive closeness is explicitly linked to Raskolnikov’s melancholy and illness.
exits: To the staircase/landing outside the landlady’s door
To the street via the building stairs
To the gateway (later, when leaving with Razumihin)
items: Window (used as a point where Razumihin and Raskolnikov talk)
Light source (lamp/candle implied by visible light through crack)

Family conflict over Luzhin and Dounia’s marriage
Zossimov consults and reassures the women
Sonia visits to invite Raskolnikov to the service at Mitrofanievsky and the funeral lunch
rooms.atmosphere: Cramped, airless, and emotionally charged; a private cell invaded by crisis and scrutiny.

rooms.name: Landing by the landlady’s door (outside Raskolnikov’s garret)
rooms.description: A fourth-storey landing where Razumihin negotiates with Pulcheria Alexandrovna and Dounia about leaving Raskolnikov undisturbed. Nastasya provides light from a step below while the conversation unfolds in whispers and agitation. The landing is also where the landlady’s door is nearby, and where later the women notice the landlady watching them through a crack. It functions as a threshold space of surveillance, persuasion, and anxious planning.
exits: Into Raskolnikov’s garret
Downstairs toward the street
To the landlady’s flat/door
items: Landlady’s door (often closed, sometimes cracked open)
characters: Praskovya Pavlovna (observing from behind her door, later)

Later, the landlady is seen spying through a crack and slams the door
rooms.atmosphere: Tense and conspiratorial; a narrow space where privacy feels impossible.

rooms.name: Landlady’s kitchen (in Raskolnikov’s building)
rooms.description: A kitchen area where Razumihin plans to spend the night on guard while Zossimov stays in the landlady’s flat. It is referenced as a practical base of operations, close enough to monitor Raskolnikov without disturbing him. The kitchen is also associated with warmth, samovar routines, and the domestic infrastructure of the lodging house. It contrasts with the garret’s tomb-like feel by implying heat and household activity.
exits: To the landlady’s flat/parlour
To the staircase/landing
Toward Raskolnikov’s garret
items: Kitchen stove (later referenced in Razumihin’s morning monologue)
events: Razumihin arranges to keep watch overnight from the passage/kitchen area
rooms.atmosphere: Domestic and utilitarian; a warm, watchful staging area amid crisis.

rooms.name: Praskovya Pavlovna’s parlour / landlady’s flat
rooms.description: The landlady’s flat includes a parlour where Zossimov spends the night, separated from the main lodging activity. Praskovya Pavlovna is described as eccentric and jealous, and she avoids direct interaction, locking herself in and refusing a personal interview. The flat is treated as a place of relative comfort (feather-bed, piano, samovar routine) compared to Raskolnikov’s garret. It also becomes part of Razumihin’s logistical plan to keep medical help close at hand.
exits: To the kitchen
To the landing/staircase
Toward Raskolnikov’s garret
items: Piano (mentioned as belonging to the landlady)
Razors left by her late husband
events: Zossimov lodges there overnight to be near Raskolnikov
Praskovya Pavlovna refuses direct contact, communicating through a closed door
rooms.atmosphere: Oddly cozy yet socially awkward; comfort mixed with eccentric hostility and jealousy.

rooms.name: Bakaleyev’s house (Pulcheria and Dounia’s lodgings)
rooms.description: A lodging house where Pulcheria Alexandrovna and Dounia stay, described as shabby and disorderly, with a ragged waiter serving tea poorly. The corridor and numbered rooms suggest a cheap, crowded establishment, and Razumihin criticizes the choice of lodgings as scandalous. It becomes the women’s base for planning the confrontation with Luzhin and for receiving updates about Raskolnikov. The setting underscores their poverty and vulnerability in Petersburg.
exits: To the street
Along the corridor to their room (number eight)
To other rooms (including a referenced Number 3 scandal site)

They receive and discuss Luzhin’s letter
They prepare to go to Raskolnikov’s garret
rooms.atmosphere: Shabby, anxious, and precarious; a temporary refuge that feels unsafe and humiliating.

rooms.name: Pulcheria and Dounia’s room (Number 8 at Bakaleyev’s house)
rooms.description: A small rented room where Pulcheria and Dounia wait anxiously for Razumihin’s reports and advice. Dounia paces with folded arms, lost in thought, while her mother sits in worry, watching her. The room is the site of reading and reacting to Luzhin’s controlling letter, and of planning the evening meeting at eight. It reflects their poverty through worn clothing and the mismatch of Dounia’s fine watch against the rest of her attire.
exits: To the corridor of Bakaleyev’s house
To the street via the building stairs
items: Dounia’s gold enamelled watch on a Venetian chain

Decision made that Raskolnikov must be present at the evening meeting
rooms.atmosphere: Tense and watchful; restrained dignity under poverty and looming confrontation.

rooms.name: Corridor at Bakaleyev’s house
rooms.description: A corridor with numbered rooms where Razumihin guides the women to their lodging and promises to return with news. It is a transitional space where he delivers rapid, emotional assurances and where he identifies their room number. The corridor is also where he later returns with Zossimov and where the women wait for footsteps and knocks. It emphasizes the impersonal, cramped nature of their accommodations.
exits: To Room No. 8 (Pulcheria and Dounia’s room)
To neighboring rooms (including No. 9 and others)
To stairs leading to street

rooms.atmosphere: Transient and exposed; privacy feels thin and dependent on closed doors.

rooms.name: Mitrofanievsky (church/cemetery area for the service)
rooms.description: A location named as the place where Marmeladov’s memorial service is to be held the next morning. It is associated with formal religious rites and the public handling of death, contrasting with the cramped tenement deathbed. Sonia delivers the invitation on Katerina Ivanovna’s behalf, making it a point of obligation and social honor. The mention situates the family’s grief within the city’s institutional rituals of burial.
exits: To the cemetery (implied by context of carrying the body and chapel)
To the Marmeladovs’ lodging (after the service, for the funeral lunch)
events: Invitation issued for the next-morning service for Marmeladov
rooms.atmosphere: Solemn and ritualized; a formal space of mourning and social duty.

rooms.name: Canal bank (near Sonia’s route home)
rooms.description: A canal-side pavement where Sonia and an unknown gentleman are briefly the only two people present. The open air contrasts with Sonia’s inward turmoil as she hurries home, preoccupied by Raskolnikov’s words and the prospect of his visit. The stranger observes her closely here, marking the beginning of his pursuit. The canal bank serves as a quiet surveillance corridor in the city.
exits: Along the canal-side pavement toward Sonia’s lodging
To side streets/turnings (where Sonia turns a corner)

Sonia remains unaware due to her preoccupation
rooms.atmosphere: Quiet, watchful, and uneasy; stillness that enables stalking and secrecy.

rooms.name: Sonia’s lodging house courtyard (where she lodges)
rooms.description: A courtyard entered through a gate from the street, where Sonia turns to the right corner toward her staircase. The unknown gentleman follows her inside, surprised by where she lives, and continues his pursuit. The courtyard acts as a semi-private space that still offers no safety from being followed. It leads directly to the stairwell and the passage on the third storey.

To the staircase up to the third storey
To the right corner leading toward Kapernaumov’s rooms

rooms.atmosphere: Exposed and vulnerable; a private residence approached like a trap.

rooms.name: Third-storey passage (Sonia’s lodging floor)
rooms.description: A passage on the third storey where Sonia walks to her door and rings at No. 9. The door bears a chalk inscription identifying the tenant: 'Kapernaumov, Tailor.' The unknown gentleman uses the passage to establish proximity, ringing next door at No. 8 and claiming to be staying nearby. The passage becomes the point where Sonia realizes she is being addressed and feels ashamed and uneasy.
exits: To No. 9 (Kapernaumov, Tailor — Sonia’s lodging)
To No. 8 (Madame Resslich’s lodging, where the stranger claims to stay)
Downstairs to the courtyard and street

The stranger introduces himself as a neighbor at No. 8
rooms.atmosphere: Narrow and intimate; a corridor where chance meetings feel threatening.

rooms.name: Kapernaumov’s (Tailor) lodging, Room No. 9
rooms.description: A room reached from the third-storey passage, marked by the chalked name 'Kapernaumov, Tailor,' where Sonia lodges. Sonia slips inside quickly when the door opens, seeking escape from the stranger’s attention. The place is implied to be modest and cramped, consistent with Sonia’s poverty and shame. It becomes a focal point for the stranger’s interest and proximity.
exits: To the third-storey passage
events: Sonia enters hurriedly after being followed
rooms.atmosphere: Hastily sought refuge; safety mixed with embarrassment and dread.

rooms.name: Madame Resslich’s lodging, Room No. 8 (next to Kapernaumov’s)
rooms.description: A neighboring lodging on the same third-storey passage, two or three yards from Sonia’s door. The unknown gentleman claims to be staying here and uses this as a pretext to speak to Sonia and normalize his presence. The room’s proximity creates an immediate sense of surveillance and unwanted familiarity. It establishes the stranger as a near neighbor with easy access to Sonia’s movements.
exits: To the third-storey passage
events: The stranger rings and claims residence, framing the encounter as coincidence
rooms.atmosphere: Unsettlingly close; a claimed foothold for intrusion.

rooms.name: Gateway of Raskolnikov’s building (tenement gateway)
rooms.description: A gateway where Raskolnikov, Razumihin, and Sonia pause after leaving Raskolnikov’s garret. It serves as a brief meeting point where directions are exchanged and Sonia explains how she found Raskolnikov via Polenka. The gateway is also where an unknown gentleman overhears Sonia mention Raskolnikov’s name and address inquiry, then notes the house and begins to wait and follow her. It functions as a threshold where private information becomes public and dangerous.

Into the building stairs leading up to Raskolnikov’s garret

rooms.atmosphere: Transitional and exposed; a place where chance overhearing changes the stakes.

rooms.name: Porfiry Petrovitch’s flat
rooms.description: A residence where Porfiry Petrovitch, the investigator connected to the murder case, can be visited directly. Raskolnikov and Razumihin enter it laughing loudly, using the noise as a kind of social mask before the encounter. The flat represents official scrutiny without being a formal police office, blending domestic space with investigative power. It is the immediate destination for discussing the redemption of pawned items and, implicitly, the murder inquiry.

To interior rooms of Porfiry’s flat (implied beyond the passage)

rooms.atmosphere: Tense beneath forced levity; a domestic threshold to interrogation and suspicion.

rooms.name: Porfiry Petrovitch’s room (investigator’s quarters)
rooms.description: A lived-in room where Porfiry Petrovitch receives visitors while wearing a dressing-gown and slippers, suggesting a semi-private, semi-official space. The room contains a sofa where Raskolnikov sits, a table used for conversation, and a window where Razumihin later stands with his back to the others. A small round table with an empty tea-glass is knocked over, sending fragments flying and heightening the tension. The setting functions as a psychological arena where Porfiry probes Raskolnikov under the guise of casual talk.
exits: Door to the passage outside (leading out to the street)

The group exits into the passage and then the street.
rooms.atmosphere: Oppressive, ironic, and performatively cordial. Beneath the banter is a sense of surveillance and psychological pressure. The room feels like a trap disguised as hospitality.

rooms.name: Passage outside Porfiry’s door
rooms.description: A transitional corridor where the visitors’ last words are exchanged after the interview. It is the space in which Porfiry’s excessive politeness continues as he sees them out. The passage marks the shift from controlled interrogation to open agitation. It also frames the moment when the conversation spills out of the room and into the public world.

rooms.name: Street outside Porfiry’s building
rooms.description: A public street where Raskolnikov and Razumihin emerge gloomy and silent after the interrogation. The open air does not relieve the tension; instead it amplifies their paranoia and argument. They walk and talk while approaching Bakaleyev’s lodgings, stopping repeatedly in heated discussion. The street becomes a moving stage for their conflicting interpretations of Porfiry’s tactics.

rooms.atmosphere: Gloomy, argumentative, and feverish. The street feels like an extension of the interrogation, with suspicion following them.

rooms.name: Bakaleyev’s lodgings (building entrance and steps)
rooms.description: The entrance area to Bakaleyev’s lodgings is reached as Razumihin and Raskolnikov near Pulcheria Alexandrovna and Dounia. The steps become a point of rupture when Raskolnikov abruptly refuses to go in and insists on leaving. Razumihin lingers on the steps, watching Raskolnikov stride away, then goes upstairs to reassure the waiting women. The location is associated with expectation, delay, and family anxiety.

Stairway up into Bakaleyev’s house (toward Pulcheria and Dounia’s rooms)

rooms.atmosphere: Strained and anticipatory. The threshold feels like a boundary between family warmth and Raskolnikov’s isolation.

rooms.name: Raskolnikov’s building gateway (tenement gateway)
rooms.description: The gateway is the passage Raskolnikov moves through dreamily after leaving his room, and later where the porter points him out to a stranger. It functions as a surveillance choke-point: people can watch who comes and goes, and strangers can inquire about tenants. The gateway frames the moment Raskolnikov is publicly identified and then pursued. It also reinforces his sense of being tracked and exposed.

Stairway up to Raskolnikov’s garret and the porter’s room

rooms.atmosphere: Exposed and ominous. The gateway feels like a checkpoint where private life becomes public knowledge.

rooms.name: Raskolnikov’s garret (his little room)
rooms.description: A cramped lodging where Raskolnikov returns in panic, drenched in sweat, and immediately fastens the latch. He rushes to the hidden hole under the paper where he had concealed items, frantically checking for anything missing. The room contains a sofa and a table, and later becomes the site of exhaustion, delirium, and intrusive visitation. It is both refuge and prison, amplifying his paranoia and physical collapse.

rooms.atmosphere: Claustrophobic, feverish, and haunted. The room feels saturated with guilt, dread, and the threat of discovery.

rooms.name: Cross-roads (where the stranger turns left)
rooms.description: A street junction where the accusing stranger and Raskolnikov reach a decisive split. The stranger turns left without looking back, then later looks back from a distance, seemingly smiling with triumph. Raskolnikov remains standing, frozen, before returning to his garret. The cross-roads symbolizes choice, pursuit, and the sudden crystallization of accusation into certainty.

rooms.atmosphere: Chilling and fateful. The open space feels like a public verdict delivered in passing.

rooms.name: Bakaleyev’s room / Pulcheria and Dounia’s lodging (meeting room with samovar)
rooms.description: A domestic room where Pulcheria Alexandrovna and Dounia receive visitors and where a samovar boils on a round table. The space becomes a battleground of manners and power as Luzhin arrives, performs dignity, and is confronted. Seating positions around the table emphasize alliances and tensions, with Raskolnikov beside his sister and Razumihin near Luzhin. The room hosts the rupture of Dounia’s engagement and the family’s shifting loyalties.

rooms.atmosphere: Initially formal and strained, then explosive and cathartic. After the rupture, it briefly turns hopeful and energetic before collapsing into alarm at Raskolnikov’s departure.

rooms.name: Corridor at Bakaleyev’s house (outside the family room)
rooms.description: A dim corridor where Raskolnikov pauses after leaving the family, and where Razumihin catches up to him. A lamp lights the space, making their silent exchange feel stark and intimate. Here, Raskolnikov issues final instructions to Razumihin to care for his mother and sister and refuses further questions. The corridor becomes the site of a wordless, mutual realization that shocks Razumihin.
exits: Door into Pulcheria and Dounia’s room
Stairs/exit out of Bakaleyev’s house
events: Raskolnikov tells Razumihin to stay with the women and not to ask him anything.
A silent moment passes where Razumihin seems to grasp a terrible hint about Raskolnikov.
Raskolnikov leaves the house.
rooms.atmosphere: Dark, intimate, and ominous. The corridor feels like a threshold where friendship turns into fearful knowledge.

rooms.name: Canal bank house where Sonia lives (old green three-storey house)
rooms.description: An old green three-storey building by the canal where Sonia lodges, reached by Raskolnikov with deliberate purpose. The porter gives vague directions to Kapernaumov the tailor, indicating a crowded, subdivided residence. The building’s courtyard and stair access feel confusing and shadowy, emphasizing secrecy and poverty. It also contains an adjacent empty room used for eavesdropping.
exits: Gate/entry from the canal-side street
Courtyard
Dark narrow staircase to upper floors
Gallery on the second storey
events: Raskolnikov arrives seeking Kapernaumov and is directed into the courtyard and stair.
rooms.atmosphere: Damp, dim, and labyrinthine. The building feels like a place where lives are stacked and overheard.

rooms.name: Sonia’s lodging house courtyard (at the canal bank house)
rooms.description: A courtyard corner where Raskolnikov finds the entrance to a dark, narrow staircase. The space is utilitarian and enclosed, serving as a funnel into the building’s interior galleries. It reinforces the sense of poverty and cramped communal living. The courtyard is also part of the route that makes Raskolnikov’s arrival feel furtive and determined.
exits: Gate to the street by the canal
Entrance to the dark narrow staircase
events: Raskolnikov locates the staircase entrance in the courtyard corner.
rooms.atmosphere: Shadowed and cramped. It feels like a back-of-house space where one slips in unnoticed.

rooms.name: Dark narrow staircase (Sonia’s building)
rooms.description: A steep, dark staircase that Raskolnikov climbs to reach the second floor. It opens onto a gallery running around the yard, suggesting a communal access design. The darkness makes him uncertain where to turn, heightening disorientation. The staircase is a physical embodiment of descent/ascent into hidden lives and moral extremity.
exits: Down to the courtyard
Up to the second floor gallery
events: Raskolnikov climbs to the second floor and emerges onto the gallery.
rooms.atmosphere: Oppressive and uncertain. The narrowness and darkness suggest secrecy and hardship.

rooms.name: Second-floor gallery over the yard (Sonia’s building)
rooms.description: An exterior-access gallery that runs around the whole second storey, overlooking the yard. Raskolnikov wanders in the darkness along it, unsure where Kapernaumov’s door is. A door opens nearby and he enters almost mechanically, leading to Sonia. The gallery functions as a liminal walkway between private rooms and communal exposure.
exits: Doors into tenants’ rooms (including Sonia’s entry)
Staircase down to the courtyard
Stair routes to other floors (implied)
events: A door opens three paces from Raskolnikov; he takes hold of it and enters.
rooms.atmosphere: Dim and tentative. The darkness makes every door feel like a threshold into danger or confession.

rooms.name: Sonia’s tiny entry (anteroom)
rooms.description: A cramped entry space where Raskolnikov first steps inside after Sonia calls out uneasily. A candle sits on a broken chair in a battered copper candlestick, providing weak light. The entry is a moment of shock and recognition for Sonia, who is frightened and overwhelmed by his sudden appearance. It serves as a narrow buffer between the public gallery and Sonia’s private room.
exits: Door back to the second-floor gallery
Opening/doorway into Sonia’s main room
events: Sonia admits Raskolnikov; he asks which room is hers and moves inside.
rooms.atmosphere: Frail and anxious. The weak candlelight underscores poverty and emotional vulnerability.

rooms.name: Sonia’s room (low-pitched, barn-like lodging)
rooms.description: A large but very low room with an irregular quadrangular shape, made grotesque by a slanting wall with three windows looking onto the canal. The walls are covered in yellow, scratched wallpaper blackened in the corners, suggesting damp and winter fumes. Sparse furnishings include a bedstead without a curtain, a plain table with a blue cloth, rush-bottom chairs, and a small chest of drawers. The room becomes a confessional space where Raskolnikov interrogates Sonia’s suffering, forces her to read the story of Lazarus, and hints he will reveal who killed Lizaveta.
exits: Door to Sonia’s tiny entry (to the gallery)
Closed door in the left wall to the Kapernaumovs’ rooms
Locked door on the right wall to the next flat (separate lodging)
items: Plain deal table with blue cloth
events: Raskolnikov arrives late at night and tells Sonia he may not see her again.
He questions her about Katerina Ivanovna, the children, and Sonia’s inability to save money.
He kisses Sonia’s foot, declaring he bows to the suffering of humanity.
Sonia reads aloud the raising of Lazarus from the Gospel of John.
Raskolnikov declares he has abandoned his family and urges Sonia to go with him.
He says he will tell Sonia who killed Lizaveta, then leaves.
rooms.atmosphere: Poor, damp, and starkly intimate. The room feels like a courtroom and a chapel at once—judgment, confession, and desperate faith under flickering light.

rooms.name: Kapernaumovs’ rooms (behind the closed door in Sonia’s room)
rooms.description: The Kapernaumovs’ living space lies behind a closed door in the left wall of Sonia’s room, indicating shared lodging arrangements. Sonia describes them as kind people, with children who often come to see her. The family’s speech impediments and poverty are emphasized, suggesting a household marked by hardship and vulnerability. Their presence nearby provides Sonia with a minimal sense of safety and community despite her isolation.
exits: Door from Sonia’s room into the Kapernaumovs’ rooms
events: Referenced as the family living adjacent to Sonia; their children visit her.
rooms.atmosphere: Crowded and humble. A sense of fragile kindness exists amid poverty and physical infirmity.

rooms.name: Next flat (separate lodging) adjoining Sonia’s room
rooms.description: A separate lodging lies beyond a door on the right-hand wall of Sonia’s room, kept locked. It forms part of the subdivided housing arrangement in the building. Though Sonia treats it as simply ‘the next flat,’ it becomes significant because an empty room there is used for covert listening. The locked boundary underscores how close strangers can be in such housing, separated only by thin walls and doors.
exits: Locked door from Sonia’s room into the next flat
events: Identified as the adjacent flat; later connected to the empty room where Svidrigaïlov listens.
rooms.atmosphere: Closed-off and uneasy. It suggests proximity without privacy.

rooms.name: Empty room adjoining Sonia’s room (in Madame Resslich’s flat)
rooms.description: A long-empty room on the other side of the dividing door, separated from Sonia’s room by the right-hand wall. It is advertised to let, with a card fixed on the gate and a notice in the canal-facing windows. Svidrigaïlov uses this vacant space as a listening post, standing at the door to overhear Sonia and Raskolnikov’s conversation. The room’s emptiness becomes a tool for intrusion and surveillance.
exits: Door to the corridor/flat area (implied)
Adjoining access to Svidrigaïlov’s own room (he carries a chair from there)
items: Advertisement notice in the windows over the canal
Card fixed on the gate (advertising to let)
events: Svidrigaïlov stands listening at the door during Sonia and Raskolnikov’s conversation.
After Raskolnikov leaves, Svidrigaïlov brings a chair to listen more comfortably in the future.
rooms.atmosphere: Silent, vacant, and predatory. The emptiness feels less like absence and more like concealment.

rooms.name: Windows over the canal (Sonia’s room / empty room frontage)
rooms.description: A set of windows looking out onto the canal, including three in Sonia’s slanted wall and additional windows where a notice is posted advertising the empty room to let. Moonlight and dim candlelight interact with these windows, shaping the room’s visibility and mood. The canal-facing aspect reinforces dampness and the sense of a cold, exposed urban edge. The windows also serve as a public-facing surface where private poverty is literally posted for rent.
items: Notice advertising a room to let (in windows over the canal)
events: Referenced as the view from Sonia’s room and as the place where the vacancy notice is displayed.
rooms.atmosphere: Bleak and watery, with light that feels intrusive rather than comforting. The canal presence suggests stagnation and chill.

rooms.name: Yusupov Garden
rooms.description: A public garden mentioned as the planned site of Berg’s balloon ascent next Sunday. It is invoked in Svidrigaïlov’s wandering, provocative conversation, suggesting fashionable spectacle and idle amusement. The garden represents a lighter, public entertainment world contrasted with the grim interiors elsewhere. Its mention also underscores Svidrigaïlov’s capriciousness and taste for novelty.
events: Svidrigaïlov mentions a balloon ride taking passengers for a fee.
rooms.atmosphere: Gossipy and theatrical by reputation. It feels like a frivolous public stage far removed from the novel’s poverty-stricken rooms.

rooms.name: Viazemsky’s house in the Hay Market
rooms.description: A house in the Hay Market area where Svidrigaïlov says he used to stay the night in earlier days. It is referenced as part of his past associations with dubious or bohemian circles. The mention situates him within a Petersburg geography of vice and transient lodging. It also hints at a social world where respectability and degradation mingle.
events: Svidrigaïlov cites it as a place he stayed in the past.
rooms.atmosphere: Seedy by implication, tied to nightlife and moral ambiguity. It carries the tone of a casual confession.

rooms.name: Hay Market
rooms.description: A district referenced as the location of Viazemsky’s house and later as the place where Sonia’s path is said to lead if she remains trapped in her life. It functions as a symbolic and social low point, associated with poverty, street life, and moral peril. The name is used as shorthand for a harsh urban reality where children and the desperate are exposed. It stands as a looming destination rather than a fully depicted scene in this excerpt.
characters: Svidrigaïlov (as speaker, indirectly via Viazemsky reference)
events: Raskolnikov tells Sonia she will ‘end in the Hay Market’ if she remains alone and trapped.
rooms.atmosphere: Harsh and degrading in implication. It is spoken of as a place of social collapse and exposure.

rooms.name: Malaya Vishera station
rooms.description: A railway station where Svidrigaïlov claims he saw Marfa Petrovna’s ghost at daybreak during his journey. The station is presented as a liminal travel point, associated with fatigue, half-waking perception, and uncanny visitation. It anchors Svidrigaïlov’s supernatural narrative in a concrete location. The mention adds a chill of unreliability and eerie coincidence to his arrival in Petersburg.
exits: Rail line onward to Petersburg (implied)
Station platforms and waiting areas (implied)
items: Pack of cards (in the ghost story)
characters: Marfa Petrovna (as apparition in his account)
events: Svidrigaïlov reports a ghostly encounter with Marfa Petrovna at daybreak.
rooms.atmosphere: Bleary and uncanny. The station feels like a threshold where exhaustion blurs into haunting.

rooms.name: America
rooms.description: A distant destination Svidrigaïlov cites as a possible elopement location in his self-justifying rhetoric. It is used to frame his pursuit of Dounia as romantic rather than predatory. The place functions more as an idea of escape and reinvention than a concrete setting. Its mention highlights the gulf between grand plans and the grim Petersburg reality.
events: Svidrigaïlov claims he once proposed eloping to America.
rooms.atmosphere: Abstract and escapist. It is invoked as a fantasy of distance and freedom.

rooms.name: Switzerland
rooms.description: Another foreign destination Svidrigaïlov mentions as part of an imagined elopement plan. Like America, it is used to dress his intentions in the language of mutual happiness and respect. The reference suggests a European refuge associated with safety and order. In context, it reads as rhetorical camouflage rather than a real plan.
events: Svidrigaïlov cites Switzerland as a possible elopement destination.
rooms.atmosphere: Idealized and distant. It functions as a polished contrast to the squalor of the present.
